title: The ULTIMATE Legs/Hamstrings Exercises Tier-List (Horse-tier to Polio-tier)
summary: Posterior chain tier list covering hamstrings, glutes and lower back, ranked from polio tier (D) to horse tier (S). Stretch-based hip hinges and knee-flexion movements win (RDL, single-leg RDL, reverse lunge, GHR, hyperextensions, kettlebell swings, lying leg curls, hip thrusts), while gimmicky glute work like band walks, donkey kicks and frog pumps is mocked. He argues the glutes and lower back don't need isolation but the hamstrings do.
claims: Quads and posterior chain get separate tier lists because a movement great for quads is usually poor for hamstrings and vice versa
Tiers: D polio (avoid), C mediocre, B decent, A excellent, S horse; pick from S and A
The squat is only C tier for the posterior chain: minimal hip hinge means little hamstring stimulus for the fatigue
Conventional and sumo deadlifts are B tier: no stretch for hamstrings and glutes, and too much lower-back fatigue for what they give
If a lift lacks the stretch component it cannot rank above decent
Barbell row is C tier for the posterior chain because the hinge is static; it does a bit of everything and nothing properly
T-bar row done heavy with knee flexion and hip hinge is a B-tier posterior chain movement and leaves hamstrings and glutes very sore
Stiff-leg deadlift (bar pushed away from midfoot, pulling with hamstrings) is A tier but lacks an emphasized negative
The Romanian deadlift is S tier in every style, bar close to shins or floated away from them
Definitions: deadlift = concentric pull from floor; stiff-leg = same with bar away from shins; RDL = negative first with bar close; stiff-leg RDL = negative first with bar floating away
Start RDLs from a rack, not by deadlifting the bar first, to set the upper back and gain reps and tension
If floating the bar away costs about 30% of your load, you have gone too far; the weight should still be under you
Do not only do RDLs: the concentric is what limits progression, so do about 80% of hinge volume with RDLs and 20% with deadlifts
Single-leg RDL is S tier and underrated: more hamstring and glute stretch than the bilateral version; use a band round the rack or a belt squat machine for balance
Banded crab walks are polio tier: garbage resistance, pattern and no stretch
Lateral step-ups are C tier: hard to load, too much balance, almost no stretch
Split squats are B tier for the posterior chain; lean the torso forward in a banana path to make them strongly glute-dominant
Single-leg hip thrust is A tier and should be loaded, not done bodyweight only
Reverse lunge is S tier: stable, safe deep range, strong stretch; go heavy and to failure
Forward lunge is polio tier for posterior chain: it is knee-dominant and people rush and rebound the negative
Lateral lunge is C tier: too much hip shift and ligament stress, hard to load
Razor curl (bent-knee Nordic/GHR) is a beginner-friendly B-tier hamstring movement
Nordic curls are A tier, not S, because they are not beginner friendly and injury prone; control the negative and don't fall and rebound
Studies he read show the glute-ham raise gives better hamstring activation than Nordics because it is more stable; GHR is S tier
Hamstrings must be trained through the stretch for hypertrophy and to avoid strains when sprinting; deadlift-only lifters get injured
Bodyweight donkey kicks push against air and do almost nothing; leg-press kickbacks are C tier and risky for the spine
Cable kickbacks are B tier: awkward ankle strap and a resistance curve that is hardest at the start
Butt blaster machine is A tier: pad in the right spot, no strength-curve problem, but few gyms have it
Kettlebell swings are S tier; science shows more hamstring activation than kickbacks; go heavy for 6-8 reps, not CrossFit style
Bodyweight booty circuits from influencers are polio tier; powerlifting women have the best glutes because they squat and deadlift heavy
Bridges are C tier but a good stepping stone if your spine is weak; as a kid he did them with plates stacked on his belly before moving to heavy lifts
Jefferson curl is B tier: a prehab exercise for spinal flexion, not a mass builder
Reverse hyperextension is A tier, a rehab movement that also builds glutes; Louie Simmons fixed his back with it; don't rebound
Back hyperextension is S tier: teaches hip hinge, easy on the lower back, progresses from bodyweight to dumbbell to barbell for years
On hyperextensions the pad goes on the upper thighs, not the hips, so the hips can hinge; snatch grip gives more range
Hip abduction machine is C tier for the posterior chain; the adductor machine is a more interesting isolation
Cable pull-through is B tier: easy to mess up and a worse swing; useful only to learn the pattern
Only isolate muscles that don't get much work from compounds; glutes and lower back grow from hinges and squats, but hamstrings often stay small in strong natural lifters
Lying leg curl is S tier and his one desired machine: full stretch, every rep is hamstring, no lower-back tax; seated curl is A tier
Lower-back isolation is pointless; heavy pulls from the floor already train it
Strong glutes and lower back matter for longevity and posture even if they need no isolation
Butt implants are polio tier; resistance training is the healthy way to a big butt, especially for women prone to weak bones
Wide, high-foot stance leg press is C tier; keep the leg press for quads
Barbell glute bridge is B tier because the floor limits range of motion
Good morning is A tier: like an RDL with the load nearer the head, so more stretch; worse risk/reward than RDLs
Core test: 10 bodyweight good mornings to parallel means good core strength
Hip thrust off a bench with full range is S tier for glutes and hamstrings; he skips it himself because his glutes are big enough
Legs need fewer exercises than upper body; get good at a couple of hip hinges
